chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Profit and Loss Statement

lessons.title: The Costs Managers Control: Fixed vs Variable Costs, Employee Costs and Overheads

children.text: An email lands from the CEO: "Every department must cut costs by 10% this quarter." Within a day, travel is frozen, the training budget is gone and someone has switched off the second air conditioner in the meeting room. Three months later, costs are down 1.4% and nobody can explain why.

The reason is that most of what a manager can see is small, and most of what is large cannot be switched off in a quarter. This lesson gives you the two classifications that matter, fixed versus variable and committed versus discretionary, and shows what each one lets you actually do.

body.text: You cannot manage a cost until you know what makes it move. Some costs follow volume, some follow time, and some follow a decision somebody made three years ago.

children.text: Fixed, Variable and the Awkward Middle
A variable cost moves with how much you produce or sell. A fixed cost stays the same within a range, whatever your volume. Most real costs sit somewhere between.

cells: Raw material, packaging, freight per consignment, sales commission, payment gateway charges, GST on inputs used
Cutting volume cuts these automatically, so they are rarely where savings come from
Factory and office rent, salaries of permanent staff, insurance, audit fees, depreciation, software licences
Cutting these needs a structural decision, not a memo
A fixed base plus a usage element
Electricity with a fixed demand charge, telecom plans, warehousing with a minimum guarantee
Attack the base and the usage separately, they are different negotiations
Fixed until volume crosses a threshold, then jumps
A second shift supervisor, another delivery van, a new warehouse
The step usually happens just before the volume that justifies it

body.text: Fixed does not mean permanent. It means it does not move with volume. Rent is fixed whether you sell one pack or ten lakh, but it is very much negotiable when the lease comes up for renewal. Managers confuse "fixed" with "untouchable" and then cut the variable costs that were never the problem.

body.title: Classify the cost
body.question: Kesari Foods pays a third party ₹18 per carton to transport snacks from its Indore plant to distributors, with no minimum commitment. How should this cost be classified?
options: Fixed, because the rate per carton is fixed
Variable, because the total moves with the number of cartons shipped
Step, because trucks come in fixed sizes
body.explanation: Classification is about the total cost, not the rate. A fixed rate per unit with no minimum commitment is the definition of a variable cost: ship nothing and you pay nothing. Add a monthly minimum guarantee and it becomes semi-variable.

children.text: Contribution and the Break-Even Point

Once costs are split into fixed and variable, one number does most of the work. Contribution is what each sale leaves behind after its own variable costs, available to cover fixed costs and then become profit.

body.latex: \text{Contribution per unit} = \text{Selling price} - \text{Variable cost per unit}
body.caption: What one more sale actually adds
The sales level at which the business exactly covers its costs

children.text: Take Kesari Foods at the unit level. A family pack sells to distributors at ₹50. Materials and packaging cost ₹26. Employee costs of ₹8 crore and other operating expenses of ₹8 crore are broadly fixed for the year.

stats.label: Annual fixed costs
stats.context: Employee ₹8 crore plus other expenses ₹8 crore

body.title: Kesari Foods: revenue and total cost as volume rises

children.text: The two lines cross a little past 66 lakh packs. Kesari actually sells one crore packs a year, so it clears break-even by a comfortable margin. The distance between where you are and where the lines cross is your margin of safety, and here it is about 33% of revenue.

body.label: Operating leverage at Kesari Foods
body.value: Contribution ₹24 crore against EBITDA ₹8 crore, a factor of 3
body.context: Above break-even, every extra rupee of contribution drops straight to EBITDA. A 10% rise in volume lifts EBITDA by about 30%. The same maths works in reverse, which is why high fixed cost businesses fall hard in a downturn.

body.title: Find the break-even
body.prompt: A Pune events company charges ₹40,000 per corporate event and incurs ₹16,000 of variable cost per event in venue and catering top-ups. Its fixed costs are ₹72 lakh a year. How many events must it run in a year to break even?
body.explanation: Contribution per event = ₹40,000 minus ₹16,000 = ₹24,000. Break-even = ₹72,00,000 ÷ ₹24,000 = 300 events, which is about 25 a month. Every event after the 300th adds ₹24,000 straight to profit.

body.title: The number that covers fixed costs
body.textWithBlank: Selling price minus variable cost per unit is called the ___ per unit.
body.explanation: Contribution first covers fixed costs, and everything beyond break-even becomes profit. It is the right number to use when deciding whether to accept an incremental order.

children.text: Employee Costs: The Line Managers Understand Least

Employee benefits expense is the largest cost line in most services businesses and the second largest in many manufacturers. It is also the line managers misquote most often, because the cost to the company, the amount credited to a bank account and the amount charged to the P&L are three different numbers.

body.title: What actually sits inside a ₹12 lakh CTC

children.text: An illustrative structure for an employee on a ₹12 lakh annual cost to company, after the new labour codes pushed wage components towards half of total remuneration.
Basic pay ₹6,00,000:
the base for provident fund, gratuity and bonus calculations.
House rent allowance ₹2,40,000:
typically set as a percentage of basic.
Special allowance ₹2,59,140:
the balancing figure that makes the package add up.
Employer provident fund contribution ₹72,000:
12% of basic pay, paid by the company on top of salary.
Gratuity provision ₹28,860:
roughly 4.81% of basic, accrued each year even though it is paid only on exit after five years of service.

The employee sees ₹10,99,140 as gross salary and takes home less after their own provident fund contribution and income tax. The P&L charges the full ₹12,00,000 across salaries and wages, contribution to provident and other funds, and gratuity. Add recruitment fees, insurance, laptops and training and the true cost of the hire is higher still.

body.text: India's four labour codes came into force on 21 November 2025 and set a common definition of wages, requiring basic pay and dearness allowance to be at least half of total remuneration. Because provident fund, gratuity and bonus are all calculated on that base, employer costs and provisions rise even when CTC is unchanged. If you approve headcount or salary structures, ask your finance and HR teams what this did to your cost per employee.

children.text: Two ratios turn headcount into something finance can discuss. Revenue per employee tells you how much output each person supports. Employee cost as a percentage of revenue tells you whether that output pays for itself. Track both, because one improves whenever you hire cheaper people and the other does not.

body.title: The 10% cost cut memo
body.scenario: You run a 90-person operations team at a Bengaluru logistics company. Your annual controllable spend is ₹14 crore: employee costs ₹9 crore, transport and fuel ₹2.6 crore, warehouse rent ₹1.4 crore, software licences ₹0.6 crore, travel ₹0.25 crore and training ₹0.15 crore. The CEO asks for a 10% cut, which is ₹1.4 crore, within the quarter.
body.prompt: Where would you look, in what order, and what would you tell the CEO cannot be done this quarter?
body.modelAnswer:
The arithmetic first: travel and training together are ₹0.4 crore. Cutting both to zero delivers less than a third of the target and damages capability. This is why visible cuts never reach the number.
Where to look, in order:
1. Variable costs tied to activity: transport and fuel at ₹2.6 crore. Route consolidation, renegotiated per-consignment rates and better load factors can plausibly yield 8% to 12%, worth ₹0.2 crore to ₹0.3 crore, and they scale with volume.
2. Contracted fixed costs where a renewal is near: software licences at ₹0.6 crore. Audit unused seats and overlapping tools. Renegotiate at renewal, not mid-term.
3. Employee cost at ₹9 crore is 64% of the spend, so no serious 10% target is met without touching it. Options in increasing severity: freeze open positions, cut overtime and contractor hours, redeploy people from low-value work, and only then consider structural change. Each has a notice period and a cost, so savings land over months, not weeks.
4. Warehouse rent at ₹1.4 crore is committed for the lease term. It becomes available only at renewal or through subletting, so exclude it from this quarter.
What to tell the CEO:
5. Give a phased number: roughly ₹0.5 crore to ₹0.6 crore achievable this quarter from variable spend, hiring freeze and licence rationalisation, with the balance needing decisions on structure or the lease.
6. Flag what the cut costs: which service levels drop, and which capability is lost if training goes.
7. Ask which is the real goal, a cash saving this quarter or a lower cost base next year. The two need completely different actions.

children.text: Overheads and the Costs You Did Not Choose

Some costs land in your department's numbers without you ever approving them. Central functions such as finance, HR, IT and the head office are real costs that have to be recovered from the businesses they support, so they are allocated out on some basis: headcount, revenue share, floor space or transaction volume.

body.title: Two ways to think about a cost you are shown

columns.label: Committed cost
points: Already locked by a contract or past decision
Lease rent, depreciation on a machine, notice-period salaries
Cannot be removed this quarter, only at renewal or exit
Argue about these when the decision is made, not after

columns.label: Discretionary cost
points: Spending you can start or stop this quarter
Easy to cut, and easiest to regret cutting
Cut with a stated recovery plan, not permanently by default

children.text: When an allocated cost lands in your P&L, ask two questions: what is the allocation basis, and does anything I control actually change it? If the answer is nothing, then the cost belongs in the conversation about company overheads, not in your team's performance review. Say so early, with the basis written down, rather than at year end.

body.title: Map your own cost base
steps: List your department's top eight costs from last year, largest first.
Tag each one as variable, fixed, semi-variable or step.
Tag each one again as committed or discretionary, and note when any contract comes up for renewal.
Compute the share of your total cost that is employee cost.
Identify which costs in your numbers are allocations from central functions, and find out the allocation basis.
Work out your contribution margin ratio if you own a product or service line, then the volume you need to cover your fixed costs.

cards.definition: A cost whose total moves with volume, such as raw material, freight per consignment or sales commission.
A cost that stays the same within a capacity range, such as rent, permanent salaries or depreciation.
A fixed base plus a usage element, such as an electricity demand charge plus units consumed.
A fixed cost that jumps when volume crosses a threshold, such as adding a second shift or another warehouse.
Selling price minus variable cost. It covers fixed costs first, then becomes profit.
The revenue or volume at which total contribution exactly equals fixed costs.
The extent to which fixed costs magnify the effect of a change in volume on profit.
Spending already locked in by a contract or past decision, which cannot be cut at short notice.

points: Variable costs move with volume, fixed costs move with decisions, and most real costs are a mix of the two.
Contribution is price minus variable cost. It covers fixed costs first, and everything after break-even is profit.
High fixed costs magnify results in both directions, which is what operating leverage means.
Employee cost is usually the largest controllable line, and cost to the company, gross salary and take-home pay are three different numbers.
The labour codes in force since 21 November 2025 raised the wage base used for provident fund, gratuity and bonus, so employer costs can rise without CTC changing.
Separate committed costs from discretionary ones before promising savings, and question the basis of any cost allocated to your team.

body.text: Kesari Foods and the Bengaluru logistics team are fictional, and the CTC structure is illustrative. Salary structures, statutory rates and labour code rules vary by state, wage level and employer, so confirm the specifics with your HR and finance teams before acting.
